operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by express revocation. Executive Order 12553 of February 25, 1986 (51 FR 7237, held govinfo text layer) has an enacting sentence reading, in part, "it is hereby ordered that the following Executive Orders, and" and, on the next line, "any amendments thereto, are revoked:" (the table row for 10045 describes creating an emergency board to investigate a railroad labor dispute). The enacting sentence has no effective-date wording and no exception or saving clause, so the first end is dated on signing, 1986-02-25 (a reading disclosed for the reviewer; the March 3, 1986 printing date is not used). Report: the held National Mediation Board copy for Emergency Board No. 71 (jobs/source-ladder/output/texts/queue_EO_10045_Actual_report_date_of_the_board_created_by_EO_10045_Presidential_Emergency_Board_Rail_40f7c1ee3a.txt, a held text lead and not an authenticated original) has no board report on the merits; it states that the board stood by until April 4, 1949, when the parties appeared in open session and reported full, complete and final disposition and settlement of all matters in dispute (the National Mediation Board index shows the case closed on April 6, 1949, an index entry and not a report date). The board therefore made no report on the merits; the report deadline and the standstill are not ends under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 (option C), and the order was functionally spent no later than April 4, 1949, the date the parties reported settlement, a date taken from the board's own record and not a date of any report. It stayed on the books until the express revocation. No earlier end is shown in held evidence.

research_rationale:
Identity: the registered original is the Federal Register printing of Executive Order 10045 at 14 FR 1227 (govinfo text layer, grade original_representation_unverified), signed March 15, 1949; the source URL is the govinfo PDF of the March 18, 1949 issue. Inventory corrected: one clause, offsets 2034 to 2876 of the held text, from the enacting words to the last operative sentence; the dossier's two spans begin at the heading and then run on into unrelated page text after the order ends. The order's heading and recitals precede it in the held text and contain no command. Text: The order recites that a dispute exists between the Wabash Railroad Company and the Ann Arbor Railroad Company, carriers, and certain of their employees represented by the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen and Enginemen, the Order of Railway Conductors and the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, labor organizations. Acting under section 10 of the Railway Labor Act, as amended (45 U.S.C. 160), it creates a board of three members, to be appointed by the President, to investigate the dispute; it bars any board member from being pecuniarily or otherwise interested in any organization of employees or any carrier; it directs the board to report its findings to the President within thirty days from the date of the order; and, as provided by section 10, it bars the Wabash Railroad Company and the Ann Arbor Railroad Company or their employees from changing, except by agreement, the conditions out of which the dispute arose, from the date of the order until thirty days after the board has made its report to the President. Ending: Executive Order 12553 of February 25, 1986 (51 FR 7237, held govinfo text layer) has an enacting sentence reading, in part, "it is hereby ordered that the following Executive Orders, and" and, on the next line, "any amendments thereto, are revoked:" (the table row for 10045 describes creating an emergency board to investigate a railroad labor dispute). The enacting sentence has no effective-date wording and no exception or saving clause, so the first end is dated on signing, 1986-02-25 (a reading disclosed for the reviewer; the March 3, 1986 printing date is not used). Report: the held National Mediation Board copy for Emergency Board No. 71 (jobs/source-ladder/output/texts/queue_EO_10045_Actual_report_date_of_the_board_created_by_EO_10045_Presidential_Emergency_Board_Rail_40f7c1ee3a.txt, a held text lead taken from a scan's text layer and not an authenticated original) is the board's report to the President. Its cover is dated April 6 (the text layer garbles the year digits; the board was appointed March 15, 1949 by this order), and its transmittal letter to the President, dated at St. Louis on April 6 and signed by the board's chairman and two members, submits the board's report as an emergency board designated under Executive Order 10045. The report recites that the board, at the parties' request, stood by until April 4, 1949, when the parties appeared in open session and reported full, complete and final disposition and settlement of all matters in dispute, evidenced by a written agreement signed on April 4, 1949; it therefore reports a settlement and makes no recommendations on the merits. The board's report to the President is accordingly dated April 6, 1949 (the date the parties reported settlement was April 4, 1949), and the standstill, which ran until thirty days after that report, ran to about May 6, 1949. Under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 (option C) the report deadline and the standstill are not ends: the order was functionally spent on April 6, 1949, when the board made its report, and its standstill period lapsed about thirty days later. It stayed on the books until the express revocation. The dossier has no citable record covering this passage, so it is stated here and not entered as a later event. Prior research: the packet locates earlier unfiled versions of this claim in another batch folder; independent review rejected them before filing (a defect in the description of the board's report, now corrected). They were read as drafts and not as evidence; no canonical claim, status hold or conflicting version exists for this order. The command was exhausted by performance and the end source is the order's own text.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10083 (14 FR 6161 (Federal Register of October 12, 1949)) was signed October 10, 1949. The filing stamp printed after the order reads October 11, 1949, one day after signing. Its held Federal Register text, registered as the original representation for this order, prints the order number, its title and the signing date, and its operative command is the sentence beginning “NOW, THEREFORE, by virtue of the authority vested in me by section 1 of the said International Organizations Immunities Act, I hereby revoke the said Executive Orders” and revoking those three orders only so far as they pertain to the three named organizations. On 2026-10-14 the command is terminated: a revoking command is complete when it takes effect, and this order states no separate effective date, so it took effect when signed on October 10, 1949. The order contains no condition, postponement, report, transfer or continuing duty. No other held text cites this order's number by an order citation. The Federal Register disposition-note search and the eCFR citation search report no hit naming this order. The packet's U.S. Code search entry also reports no hit, but the current-law table (jobs/current-law/output/ORDERS_CURRENT_LAW.csv) records one U.S. Code mention of this order (usc_mentions 1; MENTIONS.csv row usc:e410b86bce7b): the editorial note to 22 U.S.C. 288 headed 'Public International Organizations Formerly Entitled To Enjoy Certain Privileges, Exemptions, and Immunities' lists this order as the revoking order for the designations of the Inter-American Coffee Board and the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees in the part of the note the held excerpt shows (the table counts three occurrences of the order's number). That note reports the revocation as completed, with the date and Federal Register citation of this order (October 10, 1949, 14 F.R. 6161), and neither restores, extends nor ends anything; it is consistent with the end date recorded here. The U.S. Code and eCFR searches test only for current citations and are cited as bounded searches. The surviving consequence is that Executive Orders Nos. 9698, 9751 and 9823, but only so far as they designated the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, the Inter-American Coffee Board and the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees as public international organizations remains revoked; that consequence follows from the performed command and is not a command that still has to end.
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"No earlier end exists, because the only command in the order is the revocation itself and it was performed when the order took effect on October 10, 1949. The order states no effective date other than signing. The filing stamp printed after the order reads October 11, 1949, one day after signing. If the revocation were instead read as effective only on that filing, the date would be later than the date recorded here; the order text itself supplies no such rule. No later instrument is claimed as an end.","independent_command_check":"The only command is the revocation. The order creates no independent continuing duty, board, fund or authority that could outlast it; whatever the revoked instrument itself provided is outside this order and is not claimed here.","savings_check":"The revocation is a performed act whose consequence (Executive Orders Nos. 9698, 9751 and 9823, but only so far as they designated the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, the Inter-American Coffee Board and the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees as public international organizations stays revoked) survives; the held text contains no saving clause, and the bounded searches found no later order that restores or continues what was revoked. Executive Orders 9698, 9751 and 9823 remain in force as to the other organizations they designate; they are independent instruments and are not claimed here.","scope_check":"The held text has the operative inventory stated in the clause rows and no other command: no standstill, report, appointment, transfer or savings sentence. The order revokes the three earlier orders only as to the three named organizations (its recitals say those organizations have ceased to exist or are in process of liquidation), so the earlier orders continue as to every other organization they designate; that continuation belongs to those earlier orders, not to this order."}

savings_residuals.reason: The revocation is a performed act whose consequence (Executive Orders Nos. 9698, 9751 and 9823, but only so far as they designated the United Nations Relief and Rehabilitation Administration, the Inter-American Coffee Board and the Intergovernmental Committee on Refugees as public international organizations stays revoked) survives; the held text contains no saving clause, and the bounded searches found no later order that restores or continues what was revoked. Executive Orders 9698, 9751 and 9823 remain in force as to the other organizations they designate; they are independent instruments and are not claimed here.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The sole paragraph adopts existing regulations under Titles II, III and V of the Career Compensation Act of 1949 and ends with the sentence “This order shall take effect on October 1, 1949, and shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950”. Five later orders, 10098, 10118, 10136, 10158 and 10174, restated or extended that sunset; each is a later event with its own date. As last amended by Executive Order 10174 the adoption continues, for regulations under section 302 of the Act, “until January 31, 1951”, so the clause ends on January 31, 1951 (inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins). Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Each amendment takes effect the day after the earlier date it extends ends, so the dates are read inclusively and leave no gap.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10084 (14 FR 6245 (Federal Register of October 14, 1949)) concerns the order that adopts, as regulations under Titles II, III and V of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, the existing pay regulations, and fixes how long that adoption lasts. Executive Order 10084 was signed October 12, 1949 and takes effect October 1, 1949. Its sole paragraph adopts and prescribes the existing regulations under the Pay Readjustment Act of 1942, and existing departmental regulations and determinations, so far as applicable and appropriate, as regulations under Titles II, III and V of the Act, and its last sentence reads “This order shall take effect on October 1, 1949, and shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950”. Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The clause restates the last paragraph of Executive Order No. 10084 so that the order ceases to be effective on March 31, 1950 instead of January 31, 1950. Under the owner ruling on restatements the clause continues, amended, until the parent order ends. Executive Orders 10118, 10136, 10158 and 10174 restated or extended that sunset in turn, each recorded as a later event with its date; as last amended by Executive Order 10174 the parent continues, for section 302 regulations, “until January 31, 1951”, so the clause ends on January 31, 1951 (inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins). Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Each amendment takes effect the day after the earlier date it extends ends, so the dates are read inclusively and leave no gap.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10098 (15 FR 461 (Federal Register of January 27, 1950)) concerns the order that adopts, as regulations under Titles II, III and V of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, the existing pay regulations, and fixes how long that adoption lasts. Executive Order 10098 was signed January 25, 1950. Its only command amends the last paragraph of Executive Order No. 10084 to read that the order takes effect October 1, 1949 and ceases to be effective on March 31, 1950, replacing the January 31, 1950 sunset. Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Effective dates are read as follows. Executive Order 10098 and Executive Order 10118 state no effective date and are recorded as effective on their signing dates, January 25, 1950 and March 27, 1950, which fall before the January 31, 1950 and March 31, 1950 sunsets they restate, so each replaced the sunset then running. Executive Order 10136 (effective July 1, 1950) takes effect the day after June 30, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10118 continued the listed sections. Executive Order 10158 (effective September 1, 1950) takes effect the day after August 31, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10136 continued section 206, but before September 30, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10136 continued section 302, so for section 302 it replaced the September 30 date with October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (effective November 1, 1950) takes effect the day after October 31, 1950. Only Executive Orders 10136 and 10174 take effect after the date they extend. The stated end dates are read inclusively; the exclusive reading would end each continuation when its stated day begins. The last held instrument is Executive Order 10174 (15 FR 7165 (Federal Register of October 26, 1950)), which continues the order, to the extent it adopts regulations under section 302 of the Act, “until January 31, 1951”. On 2026-10-14 the clause is terminated at that last sunset, January 31, 1951, inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins. The dossier's later-event chain and the held-text search for citations of Executive Order No. 10084 (searched also with a trailing footnote digit) show no later instrument after Executive Order 10174: the Federal Register disposition-note search lists the five amendments named above, and the U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit. A later extension that the held corpus lacks is not excluded, which is the usual limit of a bounded search and is disclosed.

Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Each amendment takes effect the day after the earlier date it extends ends, so the dates are read inclusively and leave no gap. No instrument ends the parent order before January 31, 1951, and no end on a date between amendments is shown, because each amendment takes effect the day after the preceding date.","independent_command_check":"The clause has one function, which is to fix the duration of the adoption of regulations in Executive Order No. 10084, and has no separate command. Pay and allowances earned under the regulations while they were adopted are entitlements under the Career Compensation Act of 1949 and the regulations then in force; the held text creates no continuing duty after January 31, 1951, and the bounded searches found no later order continuing or restoring the adoption.","scope_check":"One operative clause: the restatement of the last paragraph of Executive Order No. 10084. savings_residuals.reason: The order's text has no saving clause. Pay and allowances earned under the regulations while they were adopted are entitlements under the Career Compensation Act of 1949 and the regulations then in force; the held text creates no continuing duty after January 31, 1951, and the bounded searches found no later order continuing or restoring the adoption.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The clause restates the last paragraph of Executive Order No. 10084 with a March 31, 1950 sunset and a proviso continuing regulations under five listed sections until June 30, 1950. Under the owner ruling on restatements the clause continues, amended, until the parent order ends. Executive Orders 10136, 10158 and 10174 extended the listed sections in turn, each recorded as a later event with its date; as last amended by Executive Order 10174 the parent continues, for section 302 regulations, “until January 31, 1951”, so the clause ends on January 31, 1951 (inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins). Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Each amendment takes effect the day after the earlier date it extends ends, so the dates are read inclusively and leave no gap.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10118 (15 FR 1767 (Federal Register of March 30, 1950)) concerns the order that adopts, as regulations under Titles II, III and V of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, the existing pay regulations, and fixes how long that adoption lasts. Executive Order 10118 was signed March 27, 1950. Its only command restates the last paragraph of Executive Order No. 10084 (as amended by Executive Order No. 10098): the order ceases to be effective on March 31, 1950, except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Act, it continues until June 30, 1950. Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Effective dates are read as follows. Executive Order 10098 and Executive Order 10118 state no effective date and are recorded as effective on their signing dates, January 25, 1950 and March 27, 1950, which fall before the January 31, 1950 and March 31, 1950 sunsets they restate, so each replaced the sunset then running. Executive Order 10136 (effective July 1, 1950) takes effect the day after June 30, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10118 continued the listed sections. Executive Order 10158 (effective September 1, 1950) takes effect the day after August 31, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10136 continued section 206, but before September 30, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10136 continued section 302, so for section 302 it replaced the September 30 date with October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (effective November 1, 1950) takes effect the day after October 31, 1950. Only Executive Orders 10136 and 10174 take effect after the date they extend. The stated end dates are read inclusively; the exclusive reading would end each continuation when its stated day begins. The last held instrument is Executive Order 10174 (15 FR 7165 (Federal Register of October 26, 1950)), which continues the order, to the extent it adopts regulations under section 302 of the Act, “until January 31, 1951”. On 2026-10-14 the clause is terminated at that last sunset, January 31, 1951, inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins. The dossier's later-event chain and the held-text search for citations of Executive Order No. 10084 (searched also with a trailing footnote digit) show no later instrument after Executive Order 10174: the Federal Register disposition-note search lists the five amendments named above, and the U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit. A later extension that the held corpus lacks is not excluded, which is the usual limit of a bounded search and is disclosed.

the conditions out of which the said dis­
pute arose.

research_rationale:
Identity: the registered original is the Federal Register printing of Executive Order 10125 at 15 FR 2391 (govinfo text layer, grade original_representation_unverified), signed April 26, 1950; the source URL is the govinfo PDF of the April 28, 1950 issue. Inventory corrected: one operative clause, offsets 1449 to the end of the sentence barring changes in conditions, from the enacting words to the last operative sentence. The dossier's span (offsets 672 to 3814) began at the order's heading and ran past the order's end, which comes at the words 'out of which the said dispute arose.' followed by the President's signature, into an unrelated Department of Agriculture regulation (Part 517, fresh apple export program, F.R. Doc. 50-3600) and the heading of Title 7 Part 201 (Federal Seed Act). The heading and the three recitals before the enacting words contain no command. Text: The order recites that a dispute exists between the Chicago & Illinois Midland Railway Company, a carrier, and certain of its employees represented by the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, a labor organization. Acting under section 10 of the Railway Labor Act, as amended (45 U.S.C. 160), it creates a board of three members, to be appointed by the President, to investigate the dispute; it bars any board member from being pecuniarily or otherwise interested in any organization of railway employees or any carrier; it directs the board to report its findings to the President within thirty days from the date of the order; and, as provided by section 10, it bars the Chicago & Illinois Midland Railway Company or its employees from changing, except by agreement, the conditions out of which the dispute arose, from the date of the order until thirty days after the board has made its report to the President. Ending: Executive Order 12553 of February 25, 1986 (51 FR 7237, held govinfo text layer) has an enacting sentence reading, in part, "it is hereby ordered that the following Executive Orders, and" and, on the next line, "any amendments thereto, are revoked:" (the table row for 10125 describes creating an emergency board to investigate a railroad labor dispute). The enacting sentence has no effective-date wording and no exception or saving clause, so the first end is dated on signing, 1986-02-25 (a reading disclosed for the reviewer; the March 3, 1986 printing date is not used). Report: the held National Mediation Board copy of the board's report (jobs/source-ladder/output/texts/queue_EO_10125_Actual_report_date_of_the_board_created_by_EO_10125_Presidential_Emergency_Board_Rail_d68f78cdf2.txt, a held text lead and not an authenticated original) has a cover page dated May 19, 1950 and a letter of transmittal to the President, signed by the board's chairman and two members (the text layer garbles the month in the letter's date line), which submits the board's report. The report deadline and the section 10 standstill are spent facts and not ends under the owner ruling of 2026-10-21 (option C): taking May 19, 1950 as the date the board made its report, the order was functionally spent on May 19, 1950 and the thirty-day period after the report ran to June 18, 1950 (a computed date, thirty days after that cover or transmittal date, not a date shown in a source); the order stayed on the books until the express revocation. The dossier has no citable record covering the report's date line, so the report date is stated here and is not entered as a later event. Prior research: the packet reports no prior claim or review for this order. Searches: current-law:usc, current-law:ecfr and later-events:ofr_catalog, each marked complete in the packet with no coverage warning; they are the packet's machine searches.
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"Earlier-end check: the order's own terms contain a thirty-day report deadline and a standstill running until thirty days after the report, neither of which is an end; no stated fixed end date or termination clause appears in the held text. The packet's bounded number search of 33,118 held texts (clause drafts excluded) found citations only in this order's own printing, the National Mediation Board report copy. The dossier's chain of later events names only Executive Order 12553 as acting on this order, and the three selected machine searches show no revoking, superseding or terminating instrument before 1986-02-25.","independent_command_check":"Independent commands: the creation of the board, the bar on interested members, the report deadline, the standstill all concern the single dispute the order addressed; none is a separate delegation, standing rule or continuing regulation. The standstill sentence restates section 10 of the Railway Labor Act, which continues on its own statutory force; the period it measures here was set by this order's creation of the board and nothing held shows it still running.","savings_check":"Savings: Executive Order 12553 contains no saving clause (the enacting sentence is followed only by the table). The order's one-time commands (creating the board, the report, the status quo period) were exhausted by performance or lapse, section 10 of the Railway Labor Act continues independently and needs no support from this order, and no surviving appointment, transfer or right is shown in any held source. State none_after_bounded_search.","scope_check":"Scope: Executive Order 12553 revokes the order by number, the table entry matches the order's subject, and the enacting sentence carries no exception, so the revocation reaches the whole order and every clause inventoried here."}

savings_residuals.reason: Executive Order 12553 revokes the order without a saving clause; the order created a board for one dispute and no surviving appointment, transfer or right is shown, and section 10 of the Railway Labor Act continues on its own force. The bounded search covered the held text of Executive Order 12553, the order's own text and the OFR catalog disposition notes.

This amendment to Part 507 contains  
the Airworthiness Directives amended or  
issued during January 1958. Individual  
notice of the Airworthiness Directives  
contained herein has been given to 4  op­
erators and other interested persons who  
are subscribers to a Civil Aeronautics

In the interest of safety, compliance  
with the notice, procedures and effective  
date provisions of section 4 of the A d­
ministrative Procedures Act is imprac­
ticable and contrary to the public inter­
est, and therefore, is not required.
Section 507.10 (a) is amended as fol­
lows:
1. 57-13-9 Piper PA-23 as it appeared  
in 23 F. R. 434 is amended by deleting

n  a line 10; Section n  c line 8 and Sec­

tives are added:
58-1-1 A ero D esign applies to all A ero  
Commander aircraft with, serial numbers 
231 through 580 except 315, 466, 471, 4 8 5 , 
492, 509, 523, 547, 568, 570, 572, 574, 576’ 
579.'
Compliance required as soon as possible  
but not later than July 1,1958.
A number of failures of the vent lines lo­
cated above the nacelle upper fire shield have  
resulted in the release of fuel and/or fuel  
vapor in the engine compartment creating a  
dangerous fire hazard. These failures are a  
result of interference or chafing between  
wing structure and the carburetor return and  
the fuel tank vent lines; Also, failures have  
occurred at the carburetor vapor return  
elbow located in the upper fire shield.
Replace the portions of the carburetor  
vapor vent and fuel tank vent lines located  
above the upper fire shield with flexible hose  
assemblies, Parts Nos. 6630086-237, 6630086-  
223, and 6630086-229, or equivalent. Securely  
fasten the hose assemblies to the wing struc­
ture with hose clamps to prevent interfer­
ence or chafing.
Replace the existing carburetor vapor re­
turn line elbows located at the upper fire  
shield with anti-rotation fittings, Part N os.  
5630085-21 and 5630085-29, and install upper  
fire shield channels, Part Nos. 5630086-25  
and 5630086-23.
(Additional details relative to this rework  
are included in Aero Design Service Bulletin  
No. 45 dated September 20,1957).
58-1-3 Convair applies to the following  
aircraft equipped with PR-58E5-17 car­
buretors in P&W Double Wasp CB16 and 
17 engines: Convair 440 serial 312  
through 420 and all CV-340 with C V -  
440 nacelles.
Compliance required by first engine over­
haul after March 1, 1958, but not later than  
October 1, 1958.
The PR-58E5— 17 carburetor setting origi­
nally provided in the aircraft has an un­
desirable leaning tendency. To overcome  
this deficiency the PR-58E5-29 carburetor  
setting has been developed and must be in­
corporated in the above aircraft.
Normal fuel metering in carburetors in­
corporating the PR-58E5— 29 “Transport 
Setting” may result in powers lower than  
those employed for aircraft certification. 
This occurs in the high power range with the 
control in the Auto-Rich position in cases 
where the carburetor meters on the rich side 
of the allowable limits. The amount of 
power loss will vary with different carburet­
ors.
Performance information in the C A A  ap­
proved Airplane Flight Manual is based upon  
the maximum certificated power ratings of  
the engine. To obtain full rated power at  
manifold pressure limits for maximum con­
tinuous power, it , is necessary to adjust the  
fuel mixture by the mixture control (takeoff

Executive Order 10753 of February 15, 1958 ends with “This order supersedes Executive Order” and names Executive Order No. 10156 of August 26, 1950 by number, date and title, replacing the succession with a new one; no savings or exception clause appears. The first end is February 15, 1958.

the Airworthiness Directives amended or  
issued during January 1958. Individual  
notice of the Airworthiness Directives  
contained herein has been given to 4  op­
erators and other interested persons who  
are subscribers to a Civil Aeronautics  
Administration mailing service.

with the notice, procedures and effective  
date provisions of section 4 of the A d­
ministrative Procedures Act is imprac­
ticable and contrary to the public inter­
est, and therefore, is not required.
Section 507.10 (a) is amended as fol­
lows:
1. 57-13-9 Piper PA-23 as it appeared  
in 23 F. R. 434 is amended by deleting  
all references to P/N 17093-00 (stabi­
lizer—fuselage attachment fitting) that  
appear in the directive; i. e., in Section  
n  a line 10; Section n  c line 8 and Sec­
tion III line 5. Reference AD 58-1-6 for  
material covering P/N 17093-00.
The f ollowing new airworthiness direc­
tives are added:
58-1-1 A ero D esign applies to all A ero  
Commander aircraft with, serial numbers 
231 through 580 except 315, 466, 471, 4 8 5 , 
492, 509, 523, 547, 568, 570, 572, 574, 576’ 
579.'
Compliance required as soon as possible  
but not later than July 1,1958.
A number of failures of the vent lines lo­
cated above the nacelle upper fire shield have  
resulted in the release of fuel and/or fuel  
vapor in the engine compartment creating a  
dangerous fire hazard. These failures are a  
result of interference or chafing between  
wing structure and the carburetor return and  
the fuel tank vent lines; Also, failures have  
occurred at the carburetor vapor return  
elbow located in the upper fire shield.
Replace the portions of the carburetor  
vapor vent and fuel tank vent lines located  
above the upper fire shield with flexible hose  
assemblies, Parts Nos. 6630086-237, 6630086-  
223, and 6630086-229, or equivalent. Securely  
fasten the hose assemblies to the wing struc­
ture with hose clamps to prevent interfer­
ence or chafing.
Replace the existing carburetor vapor re­
turn line elbows located at the upper fire  
shield with anti-rotation fittings, Part N os.  
5630085-21 and 5630085-29, and install upper  
fire shield channels, Part Nos. 5630086-25  
and 5630086-23.
(Additional details relative to this rework  
are included in Aero Design Service Bulletin  
No. 45 dated September 20,1957).
58-1-3 Convair applies to the following  
aircraft equipped with PR-58E5-17 car­
buretors in P&W Double Wasp CB16 and 
17 engines: Convair 440 serial 312  
through 420 and all CV-340 with C V -  
440 nacelles.
Compliance required by first engine over­
haul after March 1, 1958, but not later than  
October 1, 1958.
The PR-58E5— 17 carburetor setting origi­
nally provided in the aircraft has an un­
desirable leaning tendency. To overcome  
this deficiency the PR-58E5-29 carburetor  
setting has been developed and must be in­
corporated in the above aircraft.
Normal fuel metering in carburetors in­
corporating the PR-58E5— 29 “Transport 
Setting” may result in powers lower than  
those employed for aircraft certification. 
This occurs in the high power range with the 
control in the Auto-Rich position in cases 
where the carburetor meters on the rich side 
of the allowable limits. The amount of 
power loss will vary with different carburet­
ors.
Performance information in the C A A  ap­
proved Airplane Flight Manual is based upon  
the maximum certificated power ratings of  
the engine. To obtain full rated power at  
manifold pressure limits for maximum con­
tinuous power, it , is necessary to adjust the  
fuel mixture by the mixture control (takeoff  
power is not adversely affected by use of the  
full rich mixture position). P&W A Engine  
Operation Information Letter No. 28 covers  
this subject in further detail.

cated above the nacelle upper fire shield have

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10156 (15 FR 5789 (Federal Register of August 29, 1950)) was signed August 26, 1950. The held text begins with unrelated railroad-list pages of the same Federal Register issue and carries an unrelated sugar regulation after the order; the dossier's clause covered the railroad list's table fragments, so the inventory is corrected to the order's own text. The order designates, under section 179 of the Revised Statutes, the officers who perform the duties of the Secretary of the Interior in case of death, resignation, absence or sickness: the Under Secretary (1(a)), then the ranking Assistant Secretary (1(b)), then the Solicitor (1(c)); paragraph 2 defines the ranking Assistant Secretary; paragraph 3 supersedes Executive Order No. 9866 of June 14, 1947. On 2026-10-14 the designations in paragraphs 1 and 2 are terminated by Executive Order 10753 (23 FR 1107 (Federal Register of February 20, 1958)), signed February 15, 1958 by President Eisenhower, which sets a new order of succession and closes with the sentence “This order supersedes Executive Order” naming Executive Order No. 10156 of August 26, 1950 and its title. That sentence names this order by number and date and has no exception or saving clause. Paragraph 3 supersedes Executive Order No. 9866; that supersession was performed when the order took effect on August 26, 1950, which is disclosed as a candidate earlier end and not adopted, because the held bytes for it cannot be narrowed to the paragraph. The first end of paragraph 3, as of paragraphs 1 and 2, is the supersession of the whole order by Executive Order 10753 on 1958-02-15. The order has no own-terms sunset. The only later instrument in the held corpus that names the order is Executive Order 10753 (the neighbouring Federal Register page of Executive Order 10155 reprints this order's heading, not a later instrument). The Federal Register disposition-note search lists the one hit, Executive Order 10753; the eCFR citation search reports no hit. The packet's U.S. Code search entry reports no hit either, but the current-law table (jobs/current-law/output/ORDERS_CURRENT_LAW.csv) records two U.S. Code mentions of this order, both in the editorial notes to 43 U.S.C. 1451 (MENTIONS.csv rows usc:3aa65a4930ed and usc:639d9884e79e): the note for Executive Order No. 9866 says it was superseded by this order, effective August 26, 1950 (15 F.R. 5789), and the note for this order says it was superseded by Executive Order 10753, effective February 15, 1958 (23 F.R. 1107). Both notes agree with the dates recorded here and neither adds an earlier end. The superseded Executive Order No. 9866 stays superseded; that is a surviving consequence of paragraph 3 and not a command left to end.

P art 507—Airworthiness  D irectives
M ISCELLANEO US A M END M ENTS
This amendment to Part 507 contains  
the Airworthiness Directives amended or  
issued during January 1958. Individual  
notice of the Airworthiness Directives  
contained herein has been given to 4  op­
erators and other interested persons who  
are subscribers to a Civil Aeronautics  
Administration mailing service.
In the interest of safety, compliance  
with the notice, procedures and effective  
date provisions of section 4 of the A d­
ministrative Procedures Act is imprac­
ticable and contrary to the public inter­
est, and therefore, is not required.
Section 507.10 (a) is amended as fol­
lows:
1. 57-13-9 Piper PA-23 as it appeared  
in 23 F. R. 434 is amended by deleting  
all references to P/N 17093-00 (stabi­
lizer—fuselage attachment fitting) that  
appear in the directive; i. e., in Section  
n  a line 10; Section n  c line 8 and Sec­
tion III line 5. Reference AD 58-1-6 for  
material covering P/N 17093-00.
The f ollowing new airworthiness direc­
tives are added:
58-1-1 A ero D esign applies to all A ero  
Commander aircraft with, serial numbers 
231 through 580 except 315, 466, 471, 4 8 5 , 
492, 509, 523, 547, 568, 570, 572, 574, 576’ 
579.'
Compliance required as soon as possible  
but not later than July 1,1958.
A number of failures of the vent lines lo­
cated above the nacelle upper fire shield have  
resulted in the release of fuel and/or fuel  
vapor in the engine compartment creating a  
dangerous fire hazard. These failures are a  
result of interference or chafing between  
wing structure and the carburetor return and  
the fuel tank vent lines; Also, failures have  
occurred at the carburetor vapor return  
elbow located in the upper fire shield.
Replace the portions of the carburetor  
vapor vent and fuel tank vent lines located  
above the upper fire shield with flexible hose  
assemblies, Parts Nos. 6630086-237, 6630086-  
223, and 6630086-229, or equivalent. Securely  
fasten the hose assemblies to the wing struc­
ture with hose clamps to prevent interfer­
ence or chafing.
Replace the existing carburetor vapor re­
turn line elbows located at the upper fire  
shield with anti-rotation fittings, Part N os.  
5630085-21 and 5630085-29, and install upper  
fire shield channels, Part Nos. 5630086-25  
and 5630086-23.
(Additional details relative to this rework  
are included in Aero Design Service Bulletin  
No. 45 dated September 20,1957).
58-1-3 Convair applies to the following  
aircraft equipped with PR-58E5-17 car­
buretors in P&W Double Wasp CB16 and 
17 engines: Convair 440 serial 312  
through 420 and all CV-340 with C V -  
440 nacelles.
Compliance required by first engine over­
haul after March 1, 1958, but not later than  
October 1, 1958.
The PR-58E5— 17 carburetor setting origi­
nally provided in the aircraft has an un­
desirable leaning tendency. To overcome  
this deficiency the PR-58E5-29 carburetor  
setting has been developed and must be in­
corporated in the above aircraft.
Normal fuel metering in carburetors in­
corporating the PR-58E5— 29 “Transport 
Setting” may result in powers lower than  
those employed for aircraft certification. 
This occurs in the high power range with the 
control in the Auto-Rich position in cases 
where the carburetor meters on the rich side 
of the allowable limits. The amount of 
power loss will vary with different carburet­
ors.
Performance information in the C A A  ap­
proved Airplane Flight Manual is based upon  
the maximum certificated power ratings of  
the engine. To obtain full rated power at  
manifold pressure limits for maximum con­
tinuous power, it , is necessary to adjust the  
fuel mixture by the mixture control (takeoff  
power is not adversely affected by use of the  
full rich mixture position). P&W A Engine  
Operation Information Letter No. 28 covers  
this subject in further detail.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The clause continues Executive Order No. 10084, for regulations under sections 206 and 302 of the Act, until October 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950. Executive Order 10174, signed October 23, 1950 and effective November 1, 1950, restated the extension for section 302 alone until January 31, 1951, before the October 31 date arrived. Under the owner ruling on restatements the clause continues, amended, until the parent order ends, so it ends on January 31, 1951 (inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins), with Executive Order 10174 recorded as a later event. Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Each amendment takes effect the day after the earlier date it extends ends, so the dates are read inclusively and leave no gap.

research_rationale:
Executive Order 10158 (15 FR 5927 (Federal Register of September 1, 1950)) concerns the order that adopts, as regulations under Titles II, III and V of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, the existing pay regulations, and fixes how long that adoption lasts. Executive Order 10158 was signed August 31, 1950 and becomes effective September 1, 1950. Its only command amends Executive Order No. 10084 (as amended by Executive Orders No. 10098, No. 10118 and No. 10136) so that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 206 and 302 of the Act, it continues in effect until October 31, 1950. Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Effective dates are read as follows. Executive Order 10098 and Executive Order 10118 state no effective date and are recorded as effective on their signing dates, January 25, 1950 and March 27, 1950, which fall before the January 31, 1950 and March 31, 1950 sunsets they restate, so each replaced the sunset then running. Executive Order 10136 (effective July 1, 1950) takes effect the day after June 30, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10118 continued the listed sections. Executive Order 10158 (effective September 1, 1950) takes effect the day after August 31, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10136 continued section 206, but before September 30, 1950, the date to which Executive Order 10136 continued section 302, so for section 302 it replaced the September 30 date with October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (effective November 1, 1950) takes effect the day after October 31, 1950. Only Executive Orders 10136 and 10174 take effect after the date they extend. The stated end dates are read inclusively; the exclusive reading would end each continuation when its stated day begins. The last held instrument is Executive Order 10174 (15 FR 7165 (Federal Register of October 26, 1950)), which continues the order, to the extent it adopts regulations under section 302 of the Act, “until January 31, 1951”. On 2026-10-14 the clause is terminated at that last sunset, January 31, 1951, inclusive; the exclusive reading would end it when that day begins. The dossier's later-event chain and the held-text search for citations of Executive Order No. 10084 (searched also with a trailing footnote digit) show no later instrument after Executive Order 10174: the Federal Register disposition-note search lists the five amendments named above, and the U.S. Code and eCFR citation searches report no hit. A later extension that the held corpus lacks is not excluded, which is the usual limit of a bounded search and is disclosed.

Sunset text by instrument: Executive Order 10084 (October 12, 1949): the order shall cease to be effective on January 31, 1950. Executive Order 10098 (signed January 25, 1950): the last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950. Executive Order 10118 (signed March 27, 1950): last paragraph restated, ceasing March 31, 1950 except that, to the extent it adopts regulations under sections 201(e), 204, 206, 302 and 501(d) of the Career Compensation Act of 1949, it continues until June 30, 1950. Executive Order 10136 (signed June 30, 1950, effective July 1, 1950): sections 201(e), 204, 206 and 501(d) continue until August 31, 1950 and section 302 until September 30, 1950. Executive Order 10158 (signed August 31, 1950, effective September 1, 1950): sections 206 and 302 continue until October 31, 1950. Executive Order 10174 (signed October 23, 1950, effective November 1, 1950): section 302 continues until January 31, 1951. Each amendment takes effect the day after the earlier date it extends ends, so the dates are read inclusively and leave no gap. No instrument ends the parent order before January 31, 1951, and no end on a date between amendments is shown, because each amendment takes effect the day after the preceding date.","independent_command_check":"The clause has one function, which is to fix the duration of the adoption of regulations in Executive Order No. 10084, and has no separate command. The listed sections are separately sunsetted by the amendments, but the parent order as a whole ends when the last of them ends, which is the date recorded.","savings_check":"The order's text has no saving clause. Pay and allowances earned under the regulations while they were adopted are entitlements under the Career Compensation Act of 1949 and the regulations then in force; the held text creates no continuing duty after January 31, 1951, and the bounded searches found no later order continuing or restoring the adoption.","scope_check":"One operative clause: the amendment continuing sections 206 and 302 until October 31, 1950, followed by its effective-date sentence."}

savings_residuals.reason: The order's text has no saving clause. Pay and allowances earned under the regulations while they were adopted are entitlements under the Career Compensation Act of 1949 and the regulations then in force; the held text creates no continuing duty after January 31, 1951, and the bounded searches found no later order continuing or restoring the adoption.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: The operative command revokes Executive Order 2414 of June 30, 1916 and the order becomes effective at the close of business on December 31, 1953. The revocation is a one-time act, performed when the order was issued, so the clause was spent on signing, January 19, 1954; the filing date, January 20, 1954, is the alternative reading. The order's effective-date sentence dates the revocation of Executive Order 2414 back to the close of business on December 31, 1953; that is the end of the revoked order and falls before this order existed, so it is not the end of this clause. No later order is held that postpones, amends or revokes this order.

research_rationale:
EO 10514 (signed 1954-01-19 by Dwight D. Eisenhower; filed 1954-01-20, 10:29 a.m.; 19 FR 369, Federal Register of January 21, 1954 per the held source record) is read in full from the registered text jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_10514.txt; its number, title and date agree with the census register. The dossier split the order into a lead clause and a stray clause holding only the last year of the effective-date sentence; I replace them with one clause (characters 3415 to 3970 of the registered file), which holds the whole order: under the act of March 12, 1914 (38 Stat. 305) and on the Secretary of the Interior's recommendation, it revokes Executive Order 2414 of June 30, 1916 (hospital-service regulations for the construction and operation of the Government railway in Alaska, now the Alaska Railroad), and the order becomes effective at the close of business on December 31, 1953. First end: the revocation is a one-time act and was performed when the order was issued, so the clause was spent on signing, January 19, 1954; the filing date, January 20, 1954 (10:29 a.m.), is the alternative reading. The effective-date sentence makes the revocation of Executive Order 2414 effective retroactively at the close of business on December 31, 1953. That fixes when Executive Order 2414 is treated as ceasing; it cannot fix when this order's own command was performed, because this order did not exist on that date, so December 31, 1953 is the end of the revoked order and not of this one. The consequence, that Executive Order 2414 no longer applies, is a completed result and not a continuing command. Later instruments: a scan of every held order text for the bare number 10514 found only the order's own copies, the earlier orders printed in the same issue and unrelated page numbers; none amends, postpones or revokes it. Machine searches adopted after reading their coverage notes: current-law:usc (U.S. Code release point 119-121, citations of the order by number, edition through 2026-10-09, no hit), current-law:ecfr (eCFR as of 2026-10-14 and GovInfo CFR bulk, citations by number, no hit) and later-events:ofr_catalog (Office of the Federal Register disposition notes for 1937 onward plus operative sentences of saved order texts).
Member checks: {"earlier_end_check":"Nothing held amends, postpones or revokes the order. Its first end is its issuance on signing, January 19, 1954; the filing date, January 20, 1954, is the alternative reading. The retroactive effective moment stated in the order, the close of business on December 31, 1953, is the date from which the revocation of Executive Order 2414 operates and precedes this order's existence, so it is not an end of this order.","independent_command_check":"The effective-date sentence only dates the revocation; the order contains no other command.","savings_check":"None stated; the revocation is a performed act with no continuing command.","scope_check":"One clause after correcting the dossier's split of the effective-date sentence; no partial effect is held or found."}

Washington, Thursday, September 30, 1954
TITLE 3— THE PRESIDENT  
PROCLAMATION 3067  
General P ulaski ’s M emorial D ay , 1954
BY THE PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES
OF AMERICA 
A PROCLAMATION
WHEREAS Count Casimir Pulaski 
crossed the Atlantic to fight in the cause 
of freedom and gave his life for that 
cause on October 11, 1779, as a result of 
wounds received while leading the 
Pulaski Legion in a gallant cavalry 
charge at the siege of Savannah; and
WHEREAS the story of this Polish 
patriot’s supreme contribution to our 
independence is a treasured chapter in 
the annals of a grateful Nation; and
WHEREAS it is fitting that we should 
honor the memory of this distinguished 
soldier, who attained the rank of Briga­
dier General in the American Revolu­
tionary Army, on the one hundred and 
seventy-fifth anniversary of his heroic 
death:
NOW, THEREFORE, I, DW IGHT D. 
EISENHOWER, President of the United 
States of America, do hereby designate 
Monday, October 11, 1954, as General 
Pulaski’s Memorial Day, and I  invite the 
people of our country to observe the day 
with appropriate ceremonies. I  also di­
rect that the flag of the United States 
be displayed on all Government buildings 
on that day in tribute to General Casimir 
Pulaski.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, I  have 
hereunto set my hand and caused the 
Seal of the United States of America to 
be affixed.
DONE at the City of Washington this 
27th day of September in the year of 
our Lord nineteen hundred and 
[seal! fifty-four, and of the Independ­
ence of the United States of 
America the one hundred and seventy- 
ninth.

research_rationale:
EO 10563 (signed 1954-09-25 by Dwight D. Eisenhower; filed 1954-09-28, 2:14 p.m.; 19 FR 6297, Federal Register of September 30, 1954 per the held source record) is read in full from the registered text jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_10563.txt; its number, title and date agree with the census register. Inventory: one sentence, which under sections 301 and 426(c) of the Officer Personnel Act of 1947, as amended, revokes Executive Order 10266 of June 30, 1951 (suspension of certain provisions of that Act as they relate to officers of the Navy and Marine Corps). The order has no recital, effective-date wording, deadline or condition. First end: the revocation is a one-time act, so it was performed when the order took effect. With no effective-date wording the revocation is read as effective on signing, 1954-09-25; that reading is an inference from the signature block, and the filing date 1954-09-28 is the alternative. The consequence, that Executive Order 10266 no longer suspends the Act, is a completed result and not a command that continues. Later instruments: a scan of every held order text for the bare number 10563 found only the order's own copies, the next order printed in the same issue (EO 10564) and unrelated page numbers; none amends or revokes it. Held EO 10365 (signed 1952-06-24), in paragraph 3, supersedes Executive Order No. 10266 of June 30, 1951 only so far as that order relates to the suspension of the operation of provisions of the Officer Personnel Act of 1947, as amended, for commissioned officers of the Marine Corps of the grades of captain and below. That partial supersession concerns the target of this order's revocation and not this order, so it is not an end of EO 10563; it is disclosed as an earlier event narrowing what the revocation accomplished, because the suspension in Executive Order 10266 continued for the Navy officers and for the Marine Corps grades above captain until this order revoked it. Held EO 10365 (1952-06-24) superseded the target, EO 10266, in part before this order issued; it does not name EO 10563 and is not an end of it. Nothing held amends or revokes this order later.","independent_command_check":"The order has no command other than the revocation.","savings_check":"None stated; the revocation is a performed act with no continuing command.","scope_check":"One clause, the revocation sentence; no partial effect is held or found."}

THE PRESIDENT 3877
Executive Order 11332
INSPECTION OF INCOME; EXCESS-PROFITS, ESTATE, AND GIFT TAX RE­
TURNS BY THE COMMITTEE ON GOVERNMENT OPERATIONS, HOUSE  
OF REPRESENTATIVES
By virtue of the authority vested in me by section 55(a)  of the  
Internal Revenue Code of 1939, as amended (53 St at. 29,54  St at. 1008; 
26 U.S.C. (1952 Ed.) 55(a)),  and by section 6103(a) of the Internal  
Revenue Code of 1954, as amended (68A Stat. 753; 26 U.S.C. 6103(a)),  
it is hereby ordered that any income, excess-profits, estate, or gift tax  
return for the years 1947 to 1968, inclusive, shall, during the Ninetieth  
Congress, be open to inspection by the Committee on Government Op­
erations, House of Representatives, or any duly authorized subcom­
mittee thereof, in connection with its studies of the operation of  
Government activities at all levels with a view to determining the  
economy and efficiency of the Government. Such inspection shall be  
in accordance and upon compliance with the rules and regulations  
prescribed by the Secretary of the Treasury in Treasury Decisions  
6132 and 6133, relating to the inspection of returns by committees of the 
Congress, approved by the President on May 3,1955.
This order shall be effective upon its filing for publication in the  
F ederal R egister.
T he  W hite  H ouse,
March  7, 1967.
[F.R. Doc. 67-2682; Filed, Mar. 8, 1967; 10:25 a m.]
FEDERAL REGISTER, VOL. 32, NO. 46— THURSDAY, MARCH 9, 1967

research_rationale:
EO 11332 (March 7, 1967, signed by the President as printed at 32 FR 3877), read in full in the registered Federal Register text jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_11332.txt (machine-extracted text layer of the official PDF, graded original_representation_unverified and counted as an official original; I did not inspect the PDF page images). The held-text search also returns the capture file for EO 11331, which holds the same Federal Register pages (PDF page 11 of 64) and so contains this order as page text; it is not a later order. Identity: the number, subject and date in the held text agree with the census register. Content: a single operative paragraph. Under section 55(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939 and section 6103(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, it orders that any income, excess-profits, estate, or gift tax return for the years 1947 to 1968, inclusive, shall, during the Ninetieth Congress, be open to inspection by the Committee on Government Operations, House of Representatives or any duly authorized subcommittee thereof, in connection with its studies of the operation of Government activities at all levels with a view to determining the economy and efficiency of the Government; the inspection is to follow the Secretary of the Treasury rules in Treasury Decisions 6132 and 6133; and the order takes effect on filing for publication in the Federal Register. First end: by its own terms the permission operates only during the Ninetieth Congress, which ran from January 3, 1967 to January 3, 1969. Section 1 of the Twentieth Amendment ends the terms of Senators and Representatives at noon on January 3; its text is not held in this packet and the end date is taken from it as a matter of constitutional law. The end is recorded as 1969-01-03, the last day of the Congress, inclusive; the alternative reading is that the Congress ends at noon on that day. No held source lists the session dates of the 90th Congress (the held House Historian capture covers only the 80th to 89th Congresses), so no earlier candidate date is asserted. Later events: none found. The machine searches selected below (U.S. Code, eCFR and the Federal Register order catalog) have no hit for this order. A citation search of the 33,118 held order texts under jobs/*/output/texts (clause-drafts excluded) for the forms Executive Order 11332, Order No. 11332 and E.O. 11332 returns two files: the capture of the order itself (EO_11332.txt) and the capture file EO_11331.txt, which prints this order's number as neighbouring Federal Register page text; neither acts on this order. I also read the held text of EO 12553 (51 FR 7237) and its table of revoked orders does not print the number 11332. A general later revocation would in any case fall after the own-terms end. The order is read as terminated at the cutoff 2026-10-14 by its own terms; the standing disclosure that this order rests on a Federal Register OCR text layer and not on an authenticated original applies.

research_rationale:
EO 11337 (32 FR 5245; the held Federal Register text prints the date line March 26, 1967, and its filing stamp reads March 27 (the text layer garbles the month and year digits of the stamp), while the census register, the Office of the Federal Register catalog and the American Presidency Project text give March 25, 1967, which is also the packet's structured signing date; the held printing is not corrected, and the one-day difference does not affect the end, because the order took effect on its filing for publication and ends with the Ninetieth Congress), read in full in the registered Federal Register text jobs/fr-originals/data/full_run/texts/EO_11337.txt (machine-extracted text layer of the official PDF, graded original_representation_unverified and counted as an official original; I did not inspect the PDF page images). Identity: the number and subject in the held text agree with the census register; the date line differs from the register by one day, as stated above. Content: a single operative paragraph. Under section 55(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939 and section 6103(a) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954, it orders that any income, excess-profits, estate, or gift tax return for the years 1948 to 1966, inclusive, shall, during the Ninetieth Congress, be open to inspection by the Senate Committee on Government Operations or any duly authorized subcommittee thereof, in connection with its studies of the operation of Government activities at all levels with a view to determining the economy and efficiency of the Government; the inspection is to follow the Secretary of the Treasury rules in Treasury Decisions 6132 and 6133; and the order takes effect on filing for publication in the Federal Register. First end: by its own terms the permission operates only during the Ninetieth Congress, which ran from January 3, 1967 to January 3, 1969. Section 1 of the Twentieth Amendment ends the terms of Senators and Representatives at noon on January 3; its text is not held in this packet and the end date is taken from it as a matter of constitutional law. The end is recorded as 1969-01-03, the last day of the Congress, inclusive; the alternative reading is that the Congress ends at noon on that day. No held source lists the session dates of the 90th Congress (the held House Historian capture covers only the 80th to 89th Congresses), so no earlier candidate date is asserted. Later events: none found. The machine searches selected below (U.S. Code, eCFR and the Federal Register order catalog) have no hit for this order. A citation search of the 33,118 held order texts under jobs/*/output/texts (clause-drafts excluded) for the forms Executive Order 11337, Order No. 11337 and E.O. 11337 finds only the capture of the order itself. I also read the held text of EO 12553 (51 FR 7237) and its table of revoked orders does not print the number 11337. A general later revocation would in any case fall after the own-terms end. The order is read as terminated at the cutoff 2026-10-14 by its own terms; the standing disclosure that this order rests on a Federal Register OCR text layer and not on an authenticated original applies.

Nothing held amends, supersedes or revokes the order before 1969-01-03.","independent_command_check":"The only command is the inspection permission with its conditions (committee, years of returns, purpose and Treasury rules). None of these is an independent command that could outlast the Ninetieth Congress.","savings_check":"Read for savings and residual effects: none stated, and none is implied beyond completed inspections; savings state none_after_bounded_search.","scope_check":"The dossier inventory is one clause spanning the whole operative paragraph, including the sentence on effectiveness; the held text has no other operative paragraph, so the inventory is complete and no partial event exists."}

savings_residuals.reason: The order contains no savings, transition or retention language. Inspections made during the Ninetieth Congress were completed acts, and nothing in the order governs how information obtained from the returns is kept or used afterwards, so no independent command or accrued right continues after the end of the Congress.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by Executive Order 11541, signed July 1, 1970 (35 FR 10737, Federal Register of July 2, 1970). Its section 2(b) provides, in the held text, that "The organizations listed herein are terminated" and lists the Council for Urban Affairs established by this order, naming it by its Executive order number and date; its section 3 provides that "This order shall be effective July 1,1970." The termination of the Council is whole-body, not partial, and the functions heretofore assigned to the listed organizations are to be performed by the Domestic Council; the first end of every clause below is therefore July 1, 1970. This clause is the title, the enacting clause and section 1(a), which establishes the Council for Urban Affairs. It ended with the Council on the same date: it has no application once the Council it creates, staffs or constrains no longer exists, and no held source shows it continuing independently. Executive Order 12553 later revoked the whole order by number (a later event recorded on this clause, after the first end and not the end); the amendment by Executive Order 11500 changed only section 1(c) and is recorded on that clause.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by Executive Order 11541, signed July 1, 1970 (35 FR 10737, Federal Register of July 2, 1970). Its section 2(b) provides, in the held text, that "The organizations listed herein are terminated" and lists the Council for Urban Affairs established by this order, naming it by its Executive order number and date; its section 3 provides that "This order shall be effective July 1,1970." The termination of the Council is whole-body, not partial, and the functions heretofore assigned to the listed organizations are to be performed by the Domestic Council; the first end of every clause below is therefore July 1, 1970. This clause is section 1(b), under which the President presides over meetings of the Council and the Vice President presides in the President's absence. It ended with the Council on the same date: it has no application once the Council it creates, staffs or constrains no longer exists, and no held source shows it continuing independently. Executive Order 12553 later revoked the whole order by number (a later event recorded on this clause, after the first end and not the end); the amendment by Executive Order 11500 changed only section 1(c) and is recorded on that clause.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by Executive Order 11541, signed July 1, 1970 (35 FR 10737, Federal Register of July 2, 1970). Its section 2(b) provides, in the held text, that "The organizations listed herein are terminated" and lists the Council for Urban Affairs established by this order, naming it by its Executive order number and date; its section 3 provides that "This order shall be effective July 1,1970." The termination of the Council is whole-body, not partial, and the functions heretofore assigned to the listed organizations are to be performed by the Domestic Council; the first end of every clause below is therefore July 1, 1970. This clause is section 1(c), which composes the Council of the Vice President, the Attorney General, the Secretaries of Agriculture, Commerce, Labor, Health, Education, and Welfare, Housing and Urban Development and Transportation, and such other heads of departments and agencies as the President may from time to time direct. It ended with the Council on the same date: it has no application once the Council it creates, staffs or constrains no longer exists, and no held source shows it continuing independently. Later events recorded on this clause: Executive Order 11500 (signed December 12, 1969; 34 FR 19701, Federal Register of December 16, 1969) amended section 1(c) of this order before the termination by deleting its closing words that other heads of departments and agencies as the President may from time to time direct are members and inserting the same words with the words "and others" added after the words departments and agencies, so that the President could also direct persons who are not heads of departments or agencies to serve (before: other heads of departments and agencies as directed; after: other heads of departments and agencies and others as directed); it is an amendment and not an end. Executive Order 12553 (signed February 25, 1986) later revoked this order by number in its table, listing it with the subject "Establishing the Council for Urban Affairs"; because the Council had been terminated on July 1, 1970, that revocation came after the first end and is not it.

THE PRESIDENT 19701
Executive Order 11500
AMENDING EXECUTIVE ORDER NO. 11452, ESTABLISHING THE  
COUNCIL FOR URBAN AFFAIRS
By virtue of the authority vested in me by the Constitution and 
statutes of the United States, and as President of the United States, 
subsection (c) of section 1 of Executive Order No. 114521  of Janu­
ary 23, 1969, entitled “Establishing the Council for Urban Affairs” 
is amended by deleting the words “and such other heads of departments 
and agencies as the President may from time to time direct” and in­
serting in lieu thereof the following : “and such other heads of depart­
ments and agencies and others as the President may from time to time 
direct”.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by Executive Order 11541, signed July 1, 1970 (35 FR 10737, Federal Register of July 2, 1970). Its section 2(b) provides, in the held text, that "The organizations listed herein are terminated" and lists the Council for Urban Affairs established by this order, naming it by its Executive order number and date; its section 3 provides that "This order shall be effective July 1,1970." The termination of the Council is whole-body, not partial, and the functions heretofore assigned to the listed organizations are to be performed by the Domestic Council; the first end of every clause below is therefore July 1, 1970. This clause is the lead of section 2, under which the Council advises and assists the President with respect to urban affairs and performs such other duties as the President prescribes. It ended with the Council on the same date: it has no application once the Council it creates, staffs or constrains no longer exists, and no held source shows it continuing independently. Executive Order 12553 later revoked the whole order by number (a later event recorded on this clause, after the first end and not the end); the amendment by Executive Order 11500 changed only section 1(c) and is recorded on that clause.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by Executive Order 11541, signed July 1, 1970 (35 FR 10737, Federal Register of July 2, 1970). Its section 2(b) provides, in the held text, that "The organizations listed herein are terminated" and lists the Council for Urban Affairs established by this order, naming it by its Executive order number and date; its section 3 provides that "This order shall be effective July 1,1970." The termination of the Council is whole-body, not partial, and the functions heretofore assigned to the listed organizations are to be performed by the Domestic Council; the first end of every clause below is therefore July 1, 1970. This clause is section 2(1), directing the Council to assist the President in developing a national urban policy. It ended with the Council on the same date: it has no application once the Council it creates, staffs or constrains no longer exists, and no held source shows it continuing independently. Executive Order 12553 later revoked the whole order by number (a later event recorded on this clause, after the first end and not the end); the amendment by Executive Order 11500 changed only section 1(c) and is recorded on that clause.

operative_clauses.judgment_reason: Terminated by Executive Order 11541, signed July 1, 1970 (35 FR 10737, Federal Register of July 2, 1970). Its section 2(b) provides, in the held text, that "The organizations listed herein are terminated" and lists the Council for Urban Affairs established by this order, naming it by its Executive order number and date; its section 3 provides that "This order shall be effective July 1,1970." The termination of the Council is whole-body, not partial, and the functions heretofore assigned to the listed organizations are to be performed by the Domestic Council; the first end of every clause below is therefore July 1, 1970. This clause is section 2(2), directing the Council to promote the coordination of Federal programs in urban areas. It ended with the Council on the same date: it has no application once the Council it creates, staffs or constrains no longer exists, and no held source shows it continuing independently. Executive Order 12553 later revoked the whole order by number (a later event recorded on this clause, after the first end and not the end); the amendment by Executive Order 11500 changed only section 1(c) and is recorded on that clause.
